```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
```

Which documents use similar vocabulary, and which words help explain their
differences? Correspondence analysis (CA) describes a document-by-term count
table. Classical multidimensional scaling (MDS, also called principal coordinates
analysis or PCoA) represents a chosen set of document dissimilarities. The choice
of dissimilarity defines what "similar" means; a map does not establish semantic
similarity, proficiency, a causal effect, or a statistically significant group.

This guide uses **ldfreq 0.3.0.9018 or later**. Its helpers are explicitly sourced
installed examples, not exported functions. MDS uses R's `stats::cmdscale()`;
CA requires the optional `ca` package (`install.packages("ca")`). No new tokenizer
or model is needed. The example uses authored counts to make the calculations
checkable, not empirical learner differences.

## Begin with the counted documents

```{r start}
library(ldfreq)
demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "lexical-ordination-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
helper <- demo$helper
tab <- demo$tab
print(tab$documents, row.names = FALSE)
tab$active_counts
```

Seven documents contribute 45 tokens. `partial` has an unavailable selected
lemma, so its entire profile is excluded. `empty` has no source tokens,
`removed` has no selected tokens, and `outside` was not requested. These states
remain separate. `counts` retains available counts for all requested documents;
`active_counts` contains exactly the complete, nonempty profiles fitted below.
The former must not be silently substituted for the latter.

The source, original token rows and selection mask are retained. The recipe
does not normalize case or Unicode, infer lemmas, combine documents, or treat
missing labels as absence. Word identity is the exact selected string.

For your own **unchanged** `lexdiv_import_annotations()` result, load the helpers
explicitly and supply IDs and a selection rule. The
[annotation guide](annotated-corpora.html) describes source-aligned inputs.

```{r own-input, eval=FALSE}
helper <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
for (file in c("concordance.R", "lexical-ordination.R"))
  sys.source(system.file("examples", file, package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), helper)
tab <- helper$ordination_table(
  annotations, document_ids = study_document_ids,
  preprocessing_id = "lemma-exclude-punctuation-v1",
  term_col = "lemma", keep = keep,
  min_count = 1L, min_documents = 1L
)
```

`keep` has one nonmissing logical value per original token. The preprocessing
label describes a policy; it does not prove that different annotation pipelines
are equivalent. The minimum count and document-frequency thresholds use the
requested documents with complete selected terms and are applied once, before
fitting. `features` retains counts and selection decisions. A document with no
retained features remains in the audit as `no_selected_features`.

Thresholds change the analyzed vocabulary and hence the geometry. Choose them
for the research question and report them; do not tune them to make groups
separate. The default retains every term in the complete selected profiles.
The example bounds dense document-term and document-distance matrices using
`max_cells = 1e6`; it is intended for a bounded research collection.

## CA: inspect the words that define the configuration

```{r ca}
has_ca <- requireNamespace("ca", quietly = TRUE)
if (has_ca) {
  ca_result <- helper$ordination_ca(tab, k = 2)
  print(ca_result$axes)
  print(ca_result$diagnostics)
  first_axis <- subset(ca_result$columns, axis == 1)
  print(first_axis[order(first_axis$contribution, decreasing = TRUE), ], row.names = FALSE)
}
```

CA compares row profiles using column marginal frequencies and weights documents
by their token totals. Longer documents therefore have greater mass; it does
not make all documents equally influential. The `rows` and `columns` tables
report principal coordinates, mass, contribution (a proportion, not a percentage)
and cos². Contribution describes a point's role in an axis. Cos² describes how
well that axis represents the point; it is `NA` for points with numerically zero
distance to the centroid. A distant rare word need not contribute much.

```{r ca-documents}
if (has_ca) helper$ordination_plot(ca_result)
```

```{r ca-terms}
if (has_ca) helper$ordination_plot(ca_result, which = "terms", monochrome = TRUE)
```

Document and term maps are separate principal-coordinate maps. Do not compare
their plotted row-to-column distances as if they measured association. In these
authored documents, the school-related and nature-related words help explain
the dominant contrast; this is a vocabulary-composition description, not a
validated topic or ability scale. Read the contributions and cos² before naming
an axis. CA has at most `min(documents - 1, terms - 1)` nontrivial dimensions;
rank-one inputs receive a one-dimensional display. Identical profiles have no
nonzero CA inertia and are reported as not analyzable.

## MDS: choose the meaning of dissimilarity

Jaccard dissimilarity is `1 - shared types / union types`. Hellinger distance
here is the Euclidean distance between square-root relative-frequency profiles,
without the optional `1/sqrt(2)` scaling. Jaccard ignores repetition. Hellinger
retains differences in allocation among words. Neither removes the sampling
uncertainty of short documents; Jaccard also depends on the observed type sets.

```{r mds}
jaccard <- helper$ordination_mds(tab, distance = "jaccard", k = 2)
hellinger <- helper$ordination_mds(tab, distance = "hellinger", k = 2)
as.matrix(jaccard$distance)["d1", "d7"]
as.matrix(hellinger$distance)["d1", "d7"]
```

`d1` and `d7` use exactly the same types, so their Jaccard distance is zero.
Their allocation of tokens differs, so their Hellinger distance is positive.
These results answer different questions; they do not show that one distance
is universally better. The original distance object retains document labels.
Directional coverage is not a symmetric distance and is not accepted here.

```{r mds-map}
helper$ordination_plot(hellinger)
```

MDS axes are coordinates, not automatically interpretable lexical traits. Their
sign or orientation can change while all interpoint distances remain identical.
The plotting helper uses equal axis units and returns the plotted data invisibly.
Use `monochrome = TRUE` for black and white. Group labels, if added, must be
matched by document ID and do not test a group effect. Repeated observations
retain their writer/task/occasion information separately; MDS does not model
their dependence. Independently fitted maps cannot be compared by raw coordinates.

## Check what a two-dimensional map loses

```{r mds-diagnostics}
jaccard$diagnostics
hellinger$diagnostics
head(hellinger$pairs)
```

`distance_rmse` is the root mean squared difference between the original and
plotted distances. `relative_distance_error` divides their sum of squared errors
by the sum of squared original distances before taking the square root; it is
not NMDS stress. The example's Jaccard matrix has a negative eigenvalue. Its
negative magnitude relative to total absolute eigenvalue magnitude is retained,
with a relative eigenvalue tolerance of `1e-10`. No additive correction or
silent distance transformation is applied. Non-Euclidean geometry and omission
of positive dimensions can both prevent distance reconstruction. There is no
automatic acceptability threshold for the resulting map.

```{r distance-reproduction}
with(hellinger$pairs, {
  plot(original_distance, fitted_distance, asp = 1, pch = 16, col = "#0072B2",
    xlab = "Original Hellinger distance", ylab = "Distance in two-dimensional map")
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
})
```

This plot overlays the identity line on the original and reproduced distances.
Inspect pairs far from that line before interpreting local neighborhoods. All-zero
distances have no nontrivial configuration. Zero distances between some nonempty
documents are retained, not replaced by arbitrary small positive values. The
recipe exposes the requested and effective dimension counts and any recorded
rank warning from `cmdscale()`.

## Return to the evidence and save the complete analysis

```{r source-evidence}
helper$ordination_occurrences(tab, "learn")
pair <- lexdiv_term_overlap(
  colnames(tab$active_counts)[tab$active_counts["d1", ] > 0],
  colnames(tab$active_counts)[tab$active_counts["d3", ] > 0],
  document_ids = c("d1", "d3"), measures = "jaccard_types", details = "terms"
)
pair$shared_terms
pair$unique_to_a
pair$unique_to_b
```

Occurrence rows retain document, segment, token and character offsets plus the
original text. Optional context searches can use the existing
[concordance workflow](concordance-and-dispersion.html), with the saved active
token mask. The pair comparison above verifies the type-based interpretation;
it does not reproduce Hellinger distance because that distance uses frequencies.

```{r save}
record <- list(table = tab, ca = if (has_ca) ca_result else NULL,
  jaccard = jaccard, hellinger = hellinger, session = sessionInfo())
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") # Choose a persistent private path for your study.
saveRDS(record, path, version = 2)
reopened <- readRDS(path)
helper$ordination_validate(reopened$table)
helper$ordination_validate(reopened$jaccard)
stopifnot(identical(reopened, record))
```

In another R session, load the package and the two helper files as shown above,
read the saved RDS, validate its records and call
`helper$ordination_occurrences(reopened$table, "learn")` or
`helper$ordination_plot(reopened$hellinger)`. The saved table contains source
texts; keep it under the same access restrictions as those texts. A CSV of
coordinates is useful for display but does not replace this record.

A report should state the observational unit and included IDs, token/lemma and
selection policy, excluded-document counts and reasons, feature thresholds,
distance or CA weighting, dimensions, diagnostics and software versions. For
example: "We retained seven complete nonempty profiles (45 tokens), excluding
one document with a missing selected lemma, one empty source and one document
without selected tokens. We described lexical composition by CA and examined
type sharing and frequency composition with separately defined MDS distances."
Add the actual inertia and distance-reconstruction diagnostics from the saved
results and describe their implications. Do not turn this authored example into
an empirical claim about learner development.

MCA, nonmetric MDS, automatic feature/distance selection and inferential tests
are outside this recipe. CA and weighted PCoA with chi-square distances can
describe the same geometry; agreement between such maps is not independent
validation.

- Legendre, P., & Gallagher, E. D. (2001). Ecologically meaningful transformations
  for ordination of species data. *Oecologia, 129*, 271–280.
  [Transformation definitions](https://vegandevs.github.io/vegan/reference/decostand.html).
